title: The forest that was cut on purpose
teaches: Hubbard Brook, and how living plants hold a watershed’s nitrogen

blocks.text: The Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest lies in the White Mountains of New Hampshire: steep hills of maple, beech and birch, with spruce and fir near the ridgetops, cut by a row of small streams that run south into Hubbard Brook. The United States Forest Service set it aside in 1955 to study water. What made it useful was the ground beneath it. The hills are hard crystalline rock under a skin of glacial rubble, and the rock is so nearly watertight that almost all the rain and snow that fall on one small valley either go back into the air or leave by that valley's stream. The land that drains to one stream is called its **watershed**.

So each valley could be treated like a bucket with one spout. Rain gauges measured what came in. At the foot of each stream the Forest Service built a **weir**, a concrete dam with a notch cut in it[^weir], so that the depth of water in the notch told exactly how much was flowing out. A whole valley, its rock, soil, trees and animals, could be weighed by what went in and what came out, a kind of accounting no one could do in an ordinary forest, where water seeps away underground in every direction.

In 1963 two young ecologists, Gene Likens of Dartmouth College and F. Herbert Bormann, joined Forest Service hydrologists in using the weirs for something new. Likens was a chemist of lakes and streams. Every week they collected rain and stream water, and measured what was dissolved in them: calcium, potassium, sulphate and **nitrate**, one of the two forms of nitrogen plants take up from the soil. The uncut forest turned out to hold on to almost everything it got. Little more nitrogen left in its streams than arrived in the rain.

The question they wanted to answer was what the living forest was doing to hold on. The way to find out was to take it away. In the winter of 1965–66 a Forest Service crew felled every tree and shrub in one valley, Watershed 2, about 16 hectares. Nothing was dragged out; the trunks were left lying where they fell, so the soil was hardly disturbed. For the next three summers the valley was sprayed with herbicide, to stop anything growing back. Next door, Watershed 6 was left alone, with its own weir, as the comparison. The herbicide was a second change the uncut valley didn't get, and critics pointed it out; but the nitrogen in it was small beside what the stream lost, and forests cut since without herbicide have leaked nitrate too, if less.

blocks.caption: Two valleys, one cut in the winter of 1965–66 and one left standing. The lines show each stream's nitrate and its total water each year. A model, shaped to the published record.
blocks.task: Guess, then run the record past 1969

blocks.text: The first thing to change was the water. In the year after the cut, about 40 percent more water left Watershed 2 by its stream than in the years before, measured against the uncut valley. A living forest pulls water from the soil through its roots and breathes it out of its leaves as vapour, and over a summer that is a great deal of water: in these hills, more than a third of all the rain and snow. With the trees gone, it had nowhere to go but the stream.

The uncut valley is what makes the comparison honest. Wet years and dry years come and go, and both streams rise and fall with them. Only the difference between the two valleys belongs to the cutting. Ecologists call this a **paired-watershed** experiment, and it is the same reasoning as a control group in medicine.

The second change was in the chemistry. Nitrate in Watershed 2's stream began climbing in the summer of 1966 and kept climbing. By 1967 and 1968 it was running at around forty times the level in the uncut valley, at times high enough to break the American limit for drinking water. Calcium and potassium washed out several times faster too. In its worst year the cut valley lost well over a hundred kilograms of nitrogen per hectare, against a couple of kilograms from the forest next door.

Where did it come from? Not from the trees directly. The fallen leaves, twigs and roots were rotting, and the bare soil, in full sun and wetter than before, rotted faster. Decomposers break down the proteins in dead matter and release their nitrogen as **ammonium**; other soil bacteria turn ammonium into nitrate. Both had been happening all along under the living forest. The difference was that the roots had always been there to catch the nitrate as fast as it was made. With no roots, it piled up in the soil water and washed away.

Nitrate washes out so easily because of its electric charge. Soil particles, especially clay and humus, carry a negative charge on their surfaces, which holds on to positive ions like ammonium, calcium and potassium. Nitrate is a negative ion, so the soil can't hold it at all. Whatever the plants don't take, the next rain carries away.

blocks.title: An estimate
points: Water carrying 50 milligrams of nitrate per litre holds about 11 milligrams of nitrogen per litre (nitrate is about 23 percent nitrogen by weight). A metre of water running off a hectare is ten million litres. So a year of that stream carries about 110 kilograms of nitrogen out of every hectare, roughly what the cut valley lost in its worst year.

blocks.text: Nitrogen is in every protein and every strand of DNA, and four-fifths of the air is nitrogen gas. But the two atoms of a nitrogen molecule are held together by a triple bond that plants and animals can't break. Only some bacteria can, turning nitrogen gas into ammonium, and the process is called **nitrogen fixation**. Some of these bacteria live free in the soil; others live in lumps on the roots of beans, clover, lupines and alders, which feed them sugar in return[^fixers]. Lightning fixes a little more, and since the twentieth century, so do factories[^haber].

Once fixed, nitrogen goes round. Plants take up ammonium and nitrate and build proteins; animals eat the plants; leaves fall and bodies die; decomposers release ammonium again; bacteria turn it to nitrate; roots take it up. Each atom may go round many times before it leaves. The way out is through waterlogged soil, where other bacteria, short of oxygen, use nitrate in its place and turn it back into nitrogen gas: **denitrification**. Or, as at Hubbard Brook, through the stream.

blocks.caption: A forest's nitrogen as four stores and the flows between them, in kilograms per hectare. Break one step at a time and see where the nitrogen piles up and where it leaks. A model, with round numbers like a New England hardwood forest's.
blocks.task: Break each of the four steps in turn

blocks.text: Lesson 2's bathtub is at work here again. Each store fills or drains according to the gap between its inflows and outflows. Take away the plants and the nitrate store has a large inflow and only one small way out, the stream, so it fills until enough washes out to balance what the bacteria make. Take away the decomposers and the dead matter becomes a store with no outflow: nitrogen locked up in leaves and wood, and plants beside it starving.

Hubbard Brook's lesson applies to any bare ground. A vegetable bed dug over in autumn and left empty all winter is a small Watershed 2. The soil keeps rotting the summer's roots and leaves whenever it is mild, the bacteria keep making nitrate, and the winter rains carry it down past the reach of next year's roots. Farmers lose fertiliser the same way, and much of it ends up in rivers and the sea, where the next lesson takes up what it does there.

The cure is the forest's: keep something growing. A **cover crop** such as winter rye, sown after harvest, takes up nitrate through the cool months and holds it in its leaves; dug in or cut down in spring, it rots and releases the nitrogen just as the new crop needs it. A cover of clover or vetch does the same and adds fixed nitrogen too. The Soil course has the details of how a gardener keeps nitrogen in the ground.

Watershed 2 recovered. Once the spraying stopped in 1969, raspberries, pin cherries and young birches came up from seeds that had waited in the soil, and within a few years the stream's nitrate was back near normal. The regrowth took the nitrogen back up, and the water returned to the air through new leaves. Likens and Bormann's long record, and the book they wrote from it, *Pattern and Process in a Forested Ecosystem* (1979), made a point that had not been measured before: a forest's soil does not hold its nitrogen by itself. The living plants do, by catching what the soil releases.

Their records showed something else they hadn't been looking for. The rain falling on Hubbard Brook was acid, around pH 4. (On the pH scale each step down is ten times as acid; clean rain is slightly acid, at about 5.6.) That made it roughly forty times as acid as clean rain[^acid]. Their 1972 paper on it was one of the first to bring acid rain to wide notice in North America.

The valley as a unit of study has spread far beyond New Hampshire. A watershed is a natural bucket, with one way out where everything leaving can be measured, and it lets an ecologist ask what a whole landscape does with its water, carbon and nutrients. The next lesson uses a lake the same way.

blocks.caption: Six questions on nitrogen
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: After every tree in Hubbard Brook's Watershed 2 was felled, why did its stream carry about 40 percent more water?
choices: Without leaves, no water was given off as vapour, so more ran out
Snow melted faster on the open ground and ran off before freezing
Felling the trees packed the soil, so less water soaked into it
items.why: A living forest returns more than a third of the rain to the air through its leaves. With no trees, that water left by the stream instead.

items.ask: Where did most of the extra nitrate in the cut valley's stream come from?
choices: Rot and soil bacteria made it, and no roots were left to take it up
Nitrogen in the herbicide sprayed on the valley
Nitrogen fixers that spread over the bare ground
items.why: Decomposition and nitrifying bacteria went on as before, faster in warm bare soil. The difference was that no roots were catching the nitrate.

items.ask: Why does the soil hold on to ammonium and calcium but let nitrate wash away?
choices: Soil particles hold positive ions, and nitrate is a negative ion
Nitrate dissolves in water and the others don't
Bacteria break nitrate down faster than the others
items.why: Clay and humus hold positive ions on their charged surfaces. Nitrate, a negative ion, is not held and moves with the water.

items.ask: Why was a second valley left uncut beside the one that was felled?
choices: To tell changes from wet and dry years apart from the cutting's
To provide seed for the cut valley to regrow from
To measure the nitrogen the rain brought in
items.why: Weather affects both valleys alike, so only the difference between them belongs to the experiment. It is a control.

items.ask: A gardener leaves a bed bare from October to April. What does the Hubbard Brook result predict?
choices: Nitrate made in the soil over winter will wash out with the rain
The bare soil will build up nitrogen for next year's crop
Little changes, since soil bacteria stop working in winter
items.why: Rot and bacteria keep making nitrate whenever the soil is mild, and with no roots to catch it, rain carries it away. A cover crop holds it.

items.ask: In a forest's nitrogen cycle, what would happen if the decomposers stopped working?
choices: Nitrogen would pile up in dead matter, and plants would run short
Nitrate would pour out in the stream, as at Watershed 2
Plants would take more nitrogen directly from the air
items.why: Decomposers release the nitrogen in dead matter. Without them it stays locked up, and the living plants can't get enough.

summary: **Hubbard Brook's valleys work like buckets.** Watertight rock means everything leaving a valley passes its weir, where it can be measured.
**Cutting a forest sends more water down its stream.** Living leaves return more than a third of the rain to the air; without them the stream carries it.
**A cut forest leaks its nitrogen.** Rot and soil bacteria keep making nitrate; without roots to catch it, Watershed 2's stream ran about forty times the normal nitrate.
**Living plants hold a watershed's nutrients.** The soil releases them; the roots catch them before they wash away.
**Soil can't hold nitrate.** It is a negative ion, and soil particles hold only positive ones.
**Nitrogen fixers bring nitrogen in from the air; denitrifiers send it back.** Between them the same atoms go round between soil and plants many times.
**Bare ground leaks nitrate in winter.** A cover crop, like the regrowth at Hubbard Brook, catches it.
**A paired watershed is a control.** Only the difference from the uncut valley belongs to the cutting.

weir.title: Measuring a stream
weir.text: The stream backs up in a pond behind the weir and spills through a sharp-edged V-shaped notch. The flow through such a notch depends only on how deep the water stands in it, so a gauge that records the depth records the flow.

fixers.title: Fixers and their partners
fixers.text: In beans and clover the partners are bacteria called rhizobia; in alders they are a different group, Frankia. The plant builds a nodule around them, feeds them sugar and keeps oxygen low inside, since the enzyme that breaks the triple bond is spoiled by oxygen. The Botany course has the nodules.

acid.title: Acid rain
acid.text: The acid was mostly sulphuric acid, made from sulphur dioxide in smoke from power stations burning coal far to the west. After the United States cut those emissions under the Clean Air Act of 1990, the rain at Hubbard Brook became markedly less acid, though the soils, stripped of calcium, are still recovering.

haber.title: Fixing nitrogen in a factory
haber.text: Since Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch found a way to fix nitrogen with heat and pressure before the First World War, factories have made ammonia for fertiliser. Today they fix about as much nitrogen as all the bacteria on land, and roughly half the nitrogen in people's bodies has passed through the process.
